where: the closed Invited card header — the '▸ Invited 4' title, the '＋ Invite someone' affordance and the '1 suspended' badge
finding: Three elements share one 72px band and none of them shares an edge with another. The title, the trailing affordance and the badge sit on three different baselines, and the badge starts on a fourth left edge that belongs to nothing. The band reads as three fragments dropped into a box rather than one header, which is conspicuous directly above the roster card, whose header is a single clean line. It also means the card's own name is the quietest mark in its header: the red chip and the blue phrase both out-shout 'Invited'.
evidence: Baselines at 251.5, 263.5 and 277.5 CSS px — the affordance sits exactly between the title line and the badge line, aligned with neither, because it is centred against a two-line block. Left edges: the ▸ marker at 32, the card's content edge (where 'Signed-in team' and every row name start) at 33, the badge's label at 39, the title 'Invited' at 47. The roster's 'Never signed in' badge is pulled back so its label lands on 33; this one is not, and it does not land on 47 either.
direction: Decide what the header's row is. If the affordance is the title's counterpart, it belongs on the title's baseline with the badge hanging below the title as a second line; if the badge is part of the title block, the affordance should align to that block's first line rather than its optical centre. And pick one lane for the badge — either the card's content edge like the roster badge, or under the title text — not the 6px offset its own padding happens to produce.

where: the two stacked card headers — 'Invited' and 'Signed-in team'
finding: The same component insets its title differently in the two cards on the same screen. 'Invited' is jammed near its card's top edge while 'Signed-in team' floats comfortably inside its own, so two containers that are meant to be peers do not agree on their top padding. Sitting 24px apart, the disagreement is visible without measuring: one card looks tight, the other looks padded, and the difference tracks nothing the reader can name.
evidence: Cap top of the title below the card's top border: 13 CSS px in the Invited card, 22.5 in the roster card — and 17.5 for the same header on team-core. The value changes with how many lines the title block happens to hold, because a single-line title gets centred in a 44px minimum while a two- or three-line block starts at the padding. The band heights are 72 and 64, so equalising the heights was never the point; the titles landing at different distances from their frames is.
direction: Let the header's top inset be a constant and let the block grow downward from it, so a card with a badge line or a caveat line is simply taller and every title still starts at the same distance from its card's edge. The minimum-height centring is what is producing the variance, and it is buying nothing that padding would not.

where: the roster card header's two subtitle lines, 'People with a Tally profile.' and 'Outstanding invitations are not listed here.'
finding: The two lines are set at the same value with the same gap above and below, so they read as one grey paragraph rather than a description and a caveat. Worse, their sizes are ranked backwards: the line that merely restates the card title is the larger of the two, and the line that adds the fact the title does not carry is the smaller and last. The reader's eye takes the whole block as boilerplate under a heading and moves to the names.
evidence: Both lines are ink-500 (≈3.8:1 on the card) at 14px and 12px respectively, with 9.5 and 8.5 CSS px between the ink of title→line 2 and line 2→line 3 — an even three-line stack in a single tone. Every routine datum in the rows below, including the emails and the recency lines, is brighter than either. On the admin page the equivalent page-level deck was raised to ink-400 last round for exactly this reason; this card kept the older value.
direction: Rank the two lines against each other. Either the caveat steps up to the value the page deck now uses so it separates from the description, or the description — which says little the title has not — gives way so the caveat is the single line under the count. What must not persist is two lines at one tone where the more informative one is the smaller.
